lessonTitle: Research Ethics, Reproductive Ethics and Organ Donation

blocks.text: A research nurse asks a frightened man in the emergency department to sign a trial consent form while he waits for a CT scan. Two floors up, a couple considering IVF ask whether embryos can be tested before transfer, and in the transplant clinic a young woman offers a kidney to her sister. Each is a different ethical situation, but the same questions recur: is the choice free, informed and protected, and who is responsible for the safeguards?

blocks.markdown: **Research ethics** developed in response to abuses, notably those exposed after the Second World War and in later studies. Key documents include the Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report. Their shared principles are **respect for persons** (informed, voluntary consent and protection of those with reduced autonomy), **beneficence** (favourable risk-benefit balance) and **justice** (fair selection of participants and fair sharing of benefits and burdens). Research involving patients in the UK requires prior approval by an independent **Research Ethics Committee (REC)** and regulatory approvals; check current Health Research Authority requirements.

blocks.title: Clinical equipoise
blocks.text: Genuine uncertainty within the expert community about which of the arms in a trial is better. It is the ethical justification for randomisation: if one arm were known to be superior, offering a participant the inferior arm would be unethical.

items: Independent ethical review before recruitment begins, with continued oversight and reporting of serious adverse events
Informed consent: clear information on purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality and who to contact; time to consider; understanding checked
Voluntariness: no coercion, no undue inducement; refusal or withdrawal at any time without penalty or loss of usual care
Capacity: where participants lack capacity, a lawful alternative such as a consultee process is needed (check current law, including the Mental Capacity Act 2005 provisions for research)
Risk-benefit: risks minimised and justified by the value of the knowledge sought
Fair participant selection: vulnerable groups are not recruited merely for convenience

blocks.title: Reviewing a consent process
blocks.prompt: A trial of a new anticoagulant in acute stroke plans to recruit patients within hours of arrival. Many patients are drowsy or aphasic, and the team proposes that a nurse obtain written consent from whoever is at the bedside.

steps.text: Identify the problem: capacity may be impaired and the time pressure may undermine voluntariness and understanding, so consent from the patient may not be valid.

Ask whether the study has a lawful pathway for people lacking capacity, such as consent from a consultee or a legal representative, with REC approval for that approach; the protocol should say how this is done and what happens when the patient regains capacity.
Check what information is given: written and verbal summaries, plain language, time to ask questions, and the statement that refusal or later withdrawal will not affect care.
Conclude that the plan needs REC review of the consent pathway for those lacking capacity, a trained and independent person taking consent, and re-consent from participants once able.

blocks.answer: The consent process must be revised and approved by an ethics committee: consent from whoever is present is not an adequate substitute for a lawful, approved pathway.

blocks.markdown: **Pregnancy termination and assisted reproduction.** These areas involve contested moral views about the moral status of embryos and fetuses, bodily autonomy, and the role of the state. A medical student should be able to set out the main positions fairly and know the regulatory framework. In England, Wales and Scotland, termination of pregnancy is governed by the Abortion Act 1967 as amended, with grounds, gestational limits and certification requirements that are set out in law (check current law; Northern Ireland has different provisions). Clinicians may hold a **conscientious objection** to participating but must tell the patient that they can see another practitioner, must not obstruct access, and must provide emergency care (GMC guidance; check current version).

rows: Termination of pregnancy
Pregnant person's bodily autonomy and wellbeing versus claims about the moral status of the fetus
Lawful within statutory grounds; clinicians may conscientiously object but must not obstruct access; check current law
Assisted reproduction (IVF, donor gametes)
Reproductive autonomy and welfare of the child; justice in access
Regulated by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Acts (check current law)
Embryo testing and selection
Avoiding serious genetic disease versus concerns about selecting for non-medical traits
Permitted only for conditions approved by the regulator
Embryo research
Value of research versus respect due to embryos
Strictly licensed and time-limited (check current law)
Surrogacy and donor conception
Autonomy and altruism versus risks of exploitation; child's interest in knowing origins
Regulated; commercial arrangements restricted; check current law
blocks.caption: Reproductive ethics: positions and regulation. Views differ; the aim is to reason fairly, not to settle the debate.

blocks.title: Separate your own views from your duties
blocks.text: Doctors may have personal moral views, but they must not impose them on patients, must not delay or obstruct lawful care, and must give honest and non-judgemental information. Where a conscientious objection exists, the patient's access to care takes priority over the clinician's convenience.

blocks.markdown: **Organ donation and transplantation.** Donation after death includes donation after brainstem death (organs from a ventilated patient) and after circulatory death. A central safeguard is the **dead donor rule**: organs are taken only after death is confirmed by independent criteria, and the clinicians treating the patient are separate from the transplant team, with decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment taken on the patient's best interests, not on donation. In England an opt-out system applies to many adults, with exclusions and with family involvement; the other UK nations differ (check current law). Living donation is governed by the Human Tissue Act 2004 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and requires independent assessment, no payment, and a free, informed decision. Selling organs is unlawful.

rows: Main ethical safeguard
Dead donor rule; separation of treating and transplant teams
Voluntariness, understanding of risk, independent assessment
Consent
Consent or opt-out status, with family consultation
Informed consent of the donor, with the right to withdraw until surgery
Harm to donor
None after death; respect for the body and family
Operation risk, long-term risks, and psychological burdens
Allocation
Need, urgency, tissue match and expected benefit, not wealth or status
Donation may be directed to a named person or non-directed; unrelated living donation is subject to regulatory approval
Special concern
Trust in the care of dying patients
Coercion or hidden payment

blocks.title: Assessing a living kidney donor
blocks.prompt: A 35-year-old woman offers a kidney to her sister, who is on dialysis. Their mother is strongly encouraging her, and the donor mentions she 'could not live with herself' if she refused.

steps.text: Confirm capacity and understanding: explain what the operation involves, the short and long-term risks and what happens if the transplant fails, and check she can repeat this back in her own words.

Explore voluntariness: speak to her alone, away from family members, and ask whether she feels pressure. Offer a way to withdraw that does not reveal her reason to the family, such as a medical explanation if she changes her mind.
Use an independent assessor who is not the recipient's clinician to protect against conflicts of interest, and check that there is no payment or inducement.
Document the assessment, the information given and her free decision. She can withdraw at any point before surgery.

blocks.answer: Proceed only if she has capacity, understands the risks, acts freely, has been assessed independently and no payment or coercion is involved.

points: Research ethics requires independent REC approval, informed and voluntary consent with the right to withdraw, a favourable risk-benefit balance and fair participant selection; equipoise justifies randomisation.

Termination and assisted reproduction involve contested views; clinicians must practise within the law, may conscientiously object but must not obstruct access, and reproductive technologies are regulated by a statutory authority.
Organ donation depends on the dead donor rule, separation of treating and transplant teams, and fair allocation by need and benefit.
Living donation needs capacity, free and informed choice, independent assessment and no payment; trade in organs is unlawful.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of review by a Research Ethics Committee before a trial begins?

options.text: To decide which hospital will fund the study
To provide independent assessment that participants' safety, rights and dignity are protected and that the risk-benefit balance is acceptable
To guarantee that the trial will find a positive result
To obtain consent on behalf of participants

questions.correctOptionText: To provide independent assessment that participants' safety, rights and dignity are protected and that the risk-benefit balance is acceptable
questions.explanation: Independent review reduces conflicts of interest and checks that the design, consent process and risks are ethically acceptable before recruitment. It is not a guarantee of outcomes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old participant in a randomised trial tells the researcher she wants to leave the study. What is the correct response?

options.text: Persuade her to stay because incomplete data harms the study
Accept her withdrawal without penalty, ensure her usual care continues and record the decision
Ask her family to decide
Delay her request until the end of the trial

questions.correctOptionText: Accept her withdrawal without penalty, ensure her usual care continues and record the decision

distractorRationale.b: Correct: withdrawal is a right and should not affect care.
distractorRationale.d: She can withdraw at any time.

questions.explanation: Voluntariness includes the right to withdraw at any time without loss of usual care. The researcher may ask about concerns but must not pressure her.

questions.stem: What is the ethical justification for randomising participants between two treatments in a trial?

options.text: Clinical equipoise, meaning genuine expert uncertainty about which treatment is better
Convenience for the researchers
A preference for the cheaper treatment
Participants' request

questions.correctOptionText: Clinical equipoise, meaning genuine expert uncertainty about which treatment is better

distractorRationale.a: Correct: uncertainty about superiority makes randomisation ethical.
distractorRationale.b: Convenience is not an ethical justification.
distractorRationale.c: Cost alone does not justify allocation.
distractorRationale.d: Participants cannot request allocation within a randomised trial.

questions.explanation: If one arm were known to be better, randomising participants to the other would be unethical. Equipoise justifies the uncertainty on which the trial depends.

questions.stem: A study offers volunteers a very large sum of money to take part in a risky procedure, and many say the payment is their only reason. Which ethical concern is most relevant?

options.text: Undue inducement that may distort judgement about risk
Lack of equipoise
Dead donor rule
Absence of a placebo

questions.correctOptionText: Undue inducement that may distort judgement about risk

distractorRationale.a: Correct: excessive payment can lead people to accept risks they would otherwise reject.
distractorRationale.c: The dead donor rule concerns organ donation.
distractorRationale.d: A placebo is not the issue in the stem.

questions.explanation: Reimbursement for time and expense is acceptable, but payment so large that it distorts judgement threatens voluntariness. The ethics committee would examine it.

questions.stem: A GP has a conscientious objection to referring for termination of pregnancy. A patient asks for a referral. Which course is consistent with professional guidance?

options.text: Refuse and say nothing further
Tell the patient honestly that she can see another practitioner or service, ensure she can access care without delay, and not impose personal views
Refuse and warn her about the moral consequences
Pretend the request was not made

questions.correctOptionText: Tell the patient honestly that she can see another practitioner or service, ensure she can access care without delay, and not impose personal views

distractorRationale.b: Correct: objection is permitted, but patients must not be blocked.

questions.explanation: Conscientious objection allows the clinician to decline to take part, but not to obstruct access. The patient must be told how to obtain care elsewhere without delay, and the doctor must not impose personal beliefs.

questions.stem: Assisted reproduction in the UK is regulated by a statutory authority, the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The HFEA licenses and regulates fertility treatment, embryo research and storage of gametes and embryos under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Acts. Check current law for developments.

questions.stem: A couple with a known single-gene disorder ask about testing embryos before transfer in IVF. Discuss the main ethical arguments and the regulatory framework.
markingGuide: Identifies arguments for: avoiding serious disease, reproductive autonomy, preventing suffering
Identifies concerns: moral status of embryos, selection for non-medical traits, justice and access, disability perspectives
States that testing is regulated, with the regulator approving conditions for which testing is allowed
Treats the debate fairly without imposing a personal view
questions.explanation: The discussion should identify the competing values and the regulation. It should avoid a dogmatic answer, since reasonable people disagree.

questions.stem: Which arrangement best protects against a conflict of interest in organ donation after death?

options.text: The same clinicians decide on withdrawal of treatment and on retrieval of organs
The treating team is separate from the transplant team, and withdrawal decisions are made in the patient's best interests before donation is discussed
Donation is raised with the family before any prognosis is clear
Organs are allocated to the highest bidder

questions.correctOptionText: The treating team is separate from the transplant team, and withdrawal decisions are made in the patient's best interests before donation is discussed

distractorRationale.a: That would create a conflict between caring for the patient and procuring organs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: separation safeguards the patient's care and public trust.
distractorRationale.c: Raising donation prematurely may undermine trust.

questions.explanation: Separating the treating and transplant teams and basing decisions on the patient's best interests protect patients and the integrity of donation. Death must be confirmed by independent criteria before organs are retrieved.

questions.stem: Which element is most essential in assessing a potential living kidney donor?

options.text: Financial reward to encourage willingness
Free, informed decision, independent assessment and absence of payment or coercion
Agreement of family members only
Assessment by the recipient's own doctor alone

questions.correctOptionText: Free, informed decision, independent assessment and absence of payment or coercion

distractorRationale.b: Correct: voluntariness, information and independent assessment are core safeguards.
distractorRationale.c: Family agreement does not replace the donor's own decision.
distractorRationale.d: The recipient's doctor has a conflict of interest.

questions.explanation: A living donor undergoes surgery without personal medical benefit, so the safeguards are especially strict. These include capacity, a free and informed decision, independent assessment and no payment.

questions.stem: Compare the main ethical safeguards in deceased organ donation and living donation.
markingGuide: Deceased: dead donor rule with death confirmed by independent criteria
Deceased: separation of treating and transplant teams; consent or opt-out framework with family involvement
Living: capacity, voluntariness and informed consent with the right to withdraw
Living: independent assessment, absence of payment or coercion and attention to donor risk
Allocation by need and expected benefit, not wealth or status
Notes that organ trade is unlawful
questions.explanation: Deceased donation protects the dying patient and public trust; living donation protects a donor who accepts risk without medical benefit. Both depend on transparency and fair allocation.
